newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Major in first big vote without majority.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Major in first big vote without majority.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major was flying home from a tour of the Indian subcontinent on Tuesday to face the first crucial parliamentary vote since he lost his majority last month.
Members of parliament will vote (2200 GMT) on whether to approve the Finance Bill which implements the budget measures announced in November by Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke.
With defeat likely to trigger an early general election, Major was taking no chances, bringing forward the departure of his aircraft from Lahore, Pakistan by an hour.
The airliner will also be carrying two other Conservative MPs -- Trade and Industry Secretary Ian Lang and Alan Duncan -- who were accompanying Major on his six-day trip.

"Parliament is a hard taskmaster and recently scheduled parliamentary business means that I dare not fail to be back in time to vote in London this evening," Major told a seminar for Pakistani businessmen.

The government is in uncharted parliamentary waters after the loss of its majority at a by-election last month, followed by a row over claims by the two main opposition parties that it had cheated in a minor parliamentary vote.

They have suspended the parliamentary "pairing system" under which they would normally agree to one of their MPs abstaining in such a vote if Major, or another minister, was away on government business.

But Major is determined to battle on in the hope that a buoyant British economy will persuade voters to look more favourably on the Comnservatives, currrently some 20 percentage points behind the opposition Labour Party in the polls.
"I am prepared to play it long, yes. Of course I am prepared to play it long," he told reporters in Lahore who asked him about election timing.
There was little speculation in parliamentary circles about a government defeat on Tuesday.

Although they have just 323 MPs compared with 323 opposition members, the government is well placed to win key divisions as long as the nine Ulster Unionists who back British rule in Northern Ireland are prepared at least to abstain.
Labour sources said they had had no contact with the Unionists to discuss voting against the government.

One seat in the 651-seat House of Commons is at present vacant and the house speaker and three deputy speakers, all MPs, normally do not vote. A general election must be held no later than mid-May but its timing is at the government's discretion.
